description: This test validates the ability to forcefully delete directories that have been made unwritable on Mac systems. Initialize a temporary directory with a test file inside it, then verify the directory structure and confirm the directory has write permissions. Remove write permissions from the directory and verify it becomes unwritable while remaining readable, then confirm that standard deletion fails on the non-empty unwritable directory and that the contained file cannot be deleted either. Restore write permissions to allow normal cleanup of the file and directory. In a second scenario, repeat the same setup with another temporary directory and file, remove write permissions from the directory, verify standard deletion fails, then exercise the force deletion capability which should successfully remove both the unwritable directory and its contents. Assert that both the file and directory no longer exist after the forced deletion operation. The test uses JUnit 5 testing framework.

This test validates the file utility's force delete functionality when attempting to remove unwritable directories containing files on macOS systems. Initialize a temporary directory with a prefix like "dir-" and create a temporary file within it using a prefix such as "test-" and suffix ".txt". Verify the directory structure by asserting that the created path is indeed a directory and that the file's parent matches the temporary directory. Check the directory's initial write permissions to confirm it is writable, then modify the directory to be non-writable and verify this change took effect while ensuring read permissions remain intact. Attempt to delete the non-empty directory using standard file deletion methods and assert that this operation fails as expected. Try to delete the contained file directly and confirm this also fails due to the parent directory's write restrictions. Restore write permissions to the directory and successfully delete the file to demonstrate normal cleanup behavior. In a second iteration, repeat the directory and file creation process, again verify the structure and permissions, make the directory non-writable, and confirm standard deletion fails. Then invoke the file utility's force delete method on the unwritable directory and assert that both the file and directory no longer exist after the operation completes. This test uses JUnit 5 testing framework with conditional execution based on operating system.

This test validates the file listing functionality in a directory structure, specifically testing that the FileUtils listFiles method correctly identifies and returns all files matching wildcard patterns within a nested directory hierarchy. Initialize a source directory using the tempDirFile field of type File from the test class, then create a subdirectory named "list_test" within it and a further nested subdirectory named "subdir" within that, calling mkdir on both to establish the directory structure. Define an array of expected file names containing the strings "a.txt", "b.txt", "c.txt", "d.txt", "e.txt", and "f.txt", along with a corresponding array of file sizes containing the integers 123, 234, 345, 456, 678, and 789 respectively. Iterate through these arrays to create each file within the subdirectory, using TestUtils generateTestData method to populate each file with test data of the specified size via BufferedOutputStream and Files newOutputStream. Call the FileUtils listFiles method on the subdirectory, passing WildcardFileFilter instances configured with wildcards "*.*" for files and "*" for directories to retrieve all files recursively. Convert the returned Collection of File objects to an array and capture the size count. Assert that the actual file count equals the expected file names array length using assertEquals. Create a HashMap to track found file names, then iterate through the actual files array to match each file name against the expected names array, storing matches in the map. Assert that the found file names map size equals the expected file names array length to verify all expected files were discovered. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation.

Initialize a temporary directory structure and determine the default system encoding by creating a test file and extracting its encoding properties, then prepare two target files and generate a large text payload containing repeated alphabetic characters. Repeat this entire process using the builder pattern approach, configuring the writer with the same file path and encoding through the builder's fluent interface, and again execute the successful writing operation with content comparison and file existence verification. The test uses JUnit framework for assertions and validation.

description: This test validates the byte array reading functionality with bounds checking for a random access file input stream. Initialize a random access file input stream using a builder pattern, configuring it with a random access file created in read-only mode from a data file and setting the close-on-close behavior to true. Create a byte buffer with a length of 12 bytes to hold the data to be read. Call the read method on the input stream with the buffer, starting offset of zero, and the buffer length, then assert that the number of bytes read equals the expected data length of 12. Verify that the contents of the buffer match the expected byte array representation of "A Test Line." using ISO-8859-1 character encoding. Finally, assert that the available long method returns the correct remaining bytes in the file by comparing it to the total data file length minus the bytes already read. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that a queue-based input stream can properly handle bulk read operations when data is not immediately available and must wait for incoming data. Initialize a custom blocking queue that uses countdown latches to coordinate timing between read and write operations, ensuring the queue will block on polling until data becomes available. Create a queue input stream with an extended timeout duration and obtain its corresponding output stream. Execute the read operation asynchronously by launching a background task that waits for the input stream to begin polling, then writes test data to the output stream and signals completion. Perform a bulk read operation on the input stream using a byte array buffer, which should block until the background write operation provides the data. Assert that the number of bytes read matches the expected input length and that the reconstructed string content matches the original test data exactly. Verify that the asynchronous write operation completes without throwing any exceptions. The validation spans multiple inputs through parameterization. This test uses JUnit 5 testing framework.

This test validates the boundary-checking functionality of reading byte arrays from a RandomAccessFileInputStream, specifically testing that the stream correctly reads a specified number of bytes into a buffer and accurately tracks remaining available bytes. Initialize a RandomAccessFileInputStream using the builder pattern by calling the builder method, then invoke the setRandomAccessFile method with the result of calling the createRandomAccessFile helper method which creates a RandomAccessFile in READ_ONLY mode using the DATA_FILE_NAME constant, followed by calling setCloseOnClose with true to ensure the underlying file closes when the stream closes, and finally call get to construct the stream instance within a try-with-resources block. Create a byte array buffer with a length of 12 bytes to hold the data to be read. Call the read method on the RandomAccessFileInputStream with the buffer, offset 0, and length 12 to read exactly 12 bytes from the stream into the buffer starting at the beginning. Assert that the read method returns exactly 12 using assertEquals to verify the correct number of bytes were read. Validate the content of the buffer by calling assertArrayEquals to compare the buffer contents against the expected byte array representation of "A Test Line." encoded using ISO_8859_1 character set. Finally, call the availableLong method on the stream and assert using assertEquals that it returns DATA_FILE_LEN minus 12, confirming that the stream correctly calculates the remaining bytes available for reading after the 12-byte read operation. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates that reading data from a file-based input stream with specified buffer bounds correctly retrieves the expected content and accurately reports remaining available data. Initialize a specialized input stream that wraps a file opened in read-only mode, configuring it to automatically close the underlying file when the stream is closed. Create a byte buffer with a length matching the expected data size, then read data from the stream into this buffer using the bounded read operation that specifies the starting offset and number of bytes to read. Verify that the read operation returns the expected number of bytes read and that the buffer contains the exact content from the file by comparing it against the expected text encoded in a specific character set. Finally, confirm that the stream correctly calculates and reports the remaining available bytes in the file after the read operation by checking the long-form availability method. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates file age comparison functionality by checking whether files are newer or older than various time references across multiple time precision values. Initialize a temporary directory and create three test files with specific modification timestamps that establish a chronological order from oldest to newest, along with an invalid file reference that does not exist on the filesystem. Set up various time representations including dates, instants, zoned date-times, offset date-times, local date-times, local dates, and local times that correspond to specific moments in the file timeline. Execute file age comparison operations to determine if files are newer than other files and various time formats, asserting that older files return false when checked against newer references and newer files return true when compared against older references. Perform the inverse validation by checking if files are older than the same set of references, confirming that older files return true and newer files return false when compared appropriately. Verify that operations with non-existent files handle edge cases correctly by returning false for some comparisons and throwing exceptions for others. Test exception handling by confirming that null parameters and invalid file references trigger the appropriate null pointer and unchecked IO exceptions. The validation spans multiple time precision inputs through parameterization. This test uses JUnit 5 testing framework.

This parameterized test validates the bulk reading behavior of a queue input stream when data is not immediately available and the stream must wait for incoming data. Initialize two countdown latches to coordinate timing between threads, then create a custom linked blocking queue that overrides the poll method to signal when polling begins and wait for data to be written before proceeding. Build a queue input stream with the custom blocking queue and set a one-hour timeout, then obtain its corresponding queue output stream. Launch an asynchronous task that waits for the polling signal, writes the parameterized input data as UTF-8 bytes to the output stream, and signals completion. From the main thread, perform a bulk read operation on the input stream using a byte array sized to match the input data length, which will trigger the waiting behavior when no data is immediately available. Assert that the number of bytes read equals the input data length, verify that the reconstructed string from the read bytes matches the original input data, and confirm that the asynchronous writing task completes without throwing exceptions. This test uses JUnit 5 with parameterized testing via MethodSource annotation.

This test validates the bulk reading functionality of QueueInputStream when data is not immediately available and the stream must wait for data to be written asynchronously. The test uses parameterized input data and verifies that the QueueInputStream can properly handle waiting scenarios by reading the exact amount of data written to its associated QueueOutputStream. Begin by using the assumeFalse method to skip execution if the input data string is empty, then create two CountDownLatch instances named onPollLatch and afterWriteLatch, both initialized with a count of one to coordinate thread synchronization. Create a custom LinkedBlockingQueue of Integer type that overrides the poll method to count down the onPollLatch and then wait for the afterWriteLatch before proceeding with the original poll operation, simulating a delay in data availability. Initialize a QueueInputStream using the builder pattern, setting the custom blocking queue as the backing queue and configuring a timeout of one hour using Duration.ofHours, then wrap this in a try-with-resources block for automatic cleanup. Within the try block, call the newQueueOutputStream method on the QueueInputStream to obtain a connected QueueOutputStream instance. Create a CompletableFuture that runs asynchronously and waits for the onPollLatch to count down, then writes the input data bytes to the QueueOutputStream using the write method with UTF_8 encoding, and finally counts down the afterWriteLatch to signal completion. Create a byte array with length matching the input data length, then call the read method on the QueueInputStream with the byte array, offset zero, and the array length as parameters to perform the bulk read operation. Assert that the number of bytes read equals the input data length using assertEquals, then convert the read bytes back to a string using UTF_8 encoding and assert that the output string matches the original input data using assertEquals. Finally, assert that the CompletableFuture completes without throwing any exceptions using assertDoesNotThrow with the future.get method call. This test uses JUnit 5 framework with parameterized testing via ParameterizedTest and MethodSource annotations.

This test validates that CSV parsing correctly handles null column names in headers when configured to allow missing column names. Initialize a CSV format with default settings, enable header parsing, configure null string handling to treat the literal string "null" as null values, and allow missing column names in the header line. Create a CSV input containing a header row with three columns where the middle column is the literal string "null" followed by two data rows with corresponding values. Parse this CSV input using the configured format, then iterate through the parsed records to access the first record. Retrieve the parser from the record and verify that the header names list contains only the non-null column names by asserting it equals a list with just the first and third header values, and confirm that the header map size is 2, indicating that the null column name was properly excluded from the mapping. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the file utility methods for comparing file modification times against various temporal reference points using parameterized millisecond values. Initialize a temporary directory and create three test files with specific modification times calculated from the parameterized millisecond input, where an old file receives the base millisecond value, a reference file gets double that value, and a new file receives quadruple the value, with special handling for macOS Java 8 compatibility by adding an extra second. Generate empty test data for each file using buffered output streams and set their last modified times using the calculated file time values. Exercise the file utility's newer comparison method by asserting that the old file returns false when compared against the reference file and all temporal objects except when using LocalDate with midnight time combinations, and verify the new file returns true for most comparisons except when compared against future dates. Validate exception handling by asserting that null pointer exceptions are thrown for null file or temporal parameters, and unchecked IO exceptions occur when comparing against non-existent files. This test validates that a proxy writer correctly duplicates all write operations to multiple target writers simultaneously. This test validates that a tee writer correctly duplicates all write and append operations to multiple destination writers simultaneously. This test validates the TeeWriter functionality which allows writing to multiple output streams simultaneously, specifically testing that data written to a TeeWriter is correctly duplicated across all target writers. This test validates the file age comparison functionality of the FileUtils class by testing the isFileNewer and isFileOlder methods against various temporal data types and edge cases. The test creates a comprehensive scenario where file modification times are compared using different Java time representations including File objects, Date instances, millisecond timestamps, Instant, ZonedDateTime, OffsetDateTime, LocalDateTime, LocalDate, LocalTime, and OffsetTime objects to ensure the utility methods correctly determine relative file ages across all supported temporal formats. Create four File objects within the temporary directory named oldFile, refFile, newFile, and invalidFile, then convert the first three to Path objects. Convert the test FileTime to various temporal objects including Date, Instant, ZonedDateTime using system default zone, OffsetDateTime, LocalDateTime, LocalDate, LocalDate plus one day, LocalTime at midnight, and OffsetTime at UTC midnight. Create the new file similarly with test data and set its modification time to the newest FileTime. Execute comprehensive assertions testing isFileNewer method with the old file against all temporal representations expecting false results except for LocalDate with LocalTime combinations which should return true, then test the new file against the same temporal objects expecting true results except for bare LocalDate and future LocalDate combinations which should return false. Verify that calling isFileNewer with an invalid file as the first parameter returns false, and assert that calling it with an invalid file as the second parameter throws UncheckedIOException. Test the isFileOlder method with the old file against all temporal representations expecting true results except for LocalDate with time combinations which should return false, then test the new file expecting false results except for bare LocalDate and future date combinations which should return true. Verify that isFileOlder with an invalid file as the first parameter returns false and throws UncheckedIOException when the invalid file is the second parameter. Assert that both isFileNewer and isFileOlder methods throw NullPointerException when passed null File objects, null reference Files, or null Date objects, and throw UncheckedIOException when passed invalid reference files. The test uses JUnit 5 framework with ParameterizedTest and ValueSource annotations for parameterized testing and standard assertion methods.

This test validates the proxy collection writer's ability to duplicate write operations across multiple target writers by exercising various write and append methods. Initialize three string builder writers - two as targets and one as an expected reference - then create a proxy collection writer configured to write to the first two targets while passing null as a third target. Write integer values from 0 to 19 using the single character write method to both the proxy writer and expected writer, then assert that both target writers contain the same content as the expected writer. Create a character array populated with values 20 through 29 and write the entire array to both writers, followed by assertions comparing the target outputs to the expected content. Modify the array with values 25 through 34, then write a subset of 5 characters starting at offset 5 to test the partial array write method, again asserting equality between targets and expected output. Exercise the character append method by appending values 0 through 19, then create a string from the character array and append it using the character sequence append method, validating outputs after each operation. Finally, test the partial character sequence append by appending 5 characters starting at position 5 from a new string, flush the proxy writer, and verify all target writers match the expected content throughout the process. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the behavior of CSV format configuration and comment marker modification functionality by testing the withCommentMarker method's ability to create a new CSVFormat instance with a comment marker while preserving all other configuration properties. Initialize a CSVFormat instance by accessing the Default predefined format from CSVFormat.Predefined and calling getFormat to obtain the base configuration. Assert that the initial format has no escape character set using assertNull on getEscapeCharacter, verify the quote character is configured by calling assertTrue on isQuoteCharacterSet, and confirm various boolean properties are set to false including getTrim, getIgnoreSurroundingSpaces, getTrailingDelimiter, getIgnoreHeaderCase, getSkipHeaderRecord, getAllowMissingColumnNames, and isEscapeCharacterSet. Assert that the delimiter is a comma character using assertEquals with getDelimiter, verify the record separator is carriage return plus line feed using assertEquals with getRecordSeparator, confirm no comment marker is initially set using assertFalse on isCommentMarkerSet and assertNull on getCommentMarker, verify no null string is configured using assertFalse on isNullStringSet and assertNull on getNullString, confirm no quote mode is set using assertNull on getQuoteMode, verify empty lines are ignored using assertTrue on getIgnoreEmptyLines, and assert the quote character is a double quote using assertEquals with getQuoteCharacter cast to char. Create a Character object with the value 'n' and call withCommentMarker on the original format to produce a new CSVFormat instance. Re-verify all the original format's properties remain unchanged by repeating the same assertions on the original format instance. Assert the new format maintains all inherited properties by verifying isNullStringSet returns false, getAllowMissingColumnNames returns false, getQuoteCharacter returns double quote, getNullString returns null, getDelimiter returns comma, getTrailingDelimiter returns false, getIgnoreHeaderCase returns false, getTrim returns false, getEscapeCharacter returns null, isQuoteCharacterSet returns true, getIgnoreSurroundingSpaces returns false, getRecordSeparator returns carriage return plus line feed, getQuoteMode returns null, getSkipHeaderRecord returns false, isEscapeCharacterSet returns false, and getIgnoreEmptyLines returns true. Verify the comment marker was successfully set by asserting isCommentMarkerSet returns true and getCommentMarker returns 'n' when cast to char. Confirm the two format instances are distinct objects using assertNotSame in both directions and verify they are not equal using assertNotEquals from the Assertions class in both directions. Finally, validate the string representation of the new format by asserting toString returns the exact string "Delimiter=<,> QuoteChar=<"> CommentStart=<n> RecordSeparator=<\r\n> EmptyLines:ignored SkipHeaderRecord:false". This test uses the JUnit testing framework with standard assertion methods and the Assertions class for additional equality verification.

This test validates the tee functionality of a ProxyCollectionWriter that duplicates write operations across multiple StringBuilderWriter instances, ensuring that all write and append operations are correctly mirrored to each target writer. Initialize three StringBuilderWriter instances and one ProxyCollectionWriter configured with the first two StringBuilderWriter instances as targets and null as the third parameter, using try-with-resources for automatic cleanup. Execute a loop from 0 to 19, calling the write method with integer values on both the ProxyCollectionWriter and the expected StringBuilderWriter, then assert that the toString output of both target writers equals the expected writer's output with the message "ProxyCollectionWriter.write(int)". Create a character array of size 10, populate it with character values from 20 to 29 by casting integers to characters, then call the write method with the character array on both the ProxyCollectionWriter and expected writer, followed by assertions comparing the toString outputs with the message "ProxyCollectionWriter.write(char[])". Repopulate the character array with values from 25 to 34, then invoke the write method with the array, offset 5, and length 5 on both writers, asserting the toString outputs match with the message "TeeOutputStream.write(byte[], int, int)". Execute another loop from 0 to 19, calling the append method with character-cast integer values on both the ProxyCollectionWriter and expected writer, then assert the toString outputs are equal with the message "ProxyCollectionWriter.append(char)". Repopulate the character array with values 20 to 29, create a String from the array, call append with the String on both writers, and assert the outputs match with messages "ProxyCollectionWriter.append(CharSequence)" and "ProxyCollectionWriter.write(CharSequence)". Repopulate the array with values 25 to 34, create a String from the array, call append with the String, start index 5, and end index 5 on both writers, then assert the toString outputs are equal with the message "ProxyCollectionWriter.append(CharSequence, int, int)". Call flush and close on the expected writer, then call flush on the ProxyCollectionWriter before the try-with-resources block automatically closes all resources. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

Initialize a CSV format with default settings and configure it to use a backslash as the escape character by calling the format builder's escape method. Create a string writer to capture output, then instantiate a CSV printer with the writer and format within a try-with-resources block. Use the printer to write a record containing two values: a string with "foo" followed by a backslash, and the string "bar". After the printer closes, create a string reader from the writer's output content and establish a CSV parser using the same format configuration within another try-with-resources block. Parse all records from the input and iterate through each record to assert that the first field equals "foo \\" and the second field equals "bar", validating that the escape character properly handles backslash characters during the round-trip write and read process. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the CSV parser's ability to handle multi-character delimiters with escape sequences. Initialize a CSV format using the default configuration, then configure it with a multi-character delimiter string "[|]" and set the escape character to '!'. Create a string containing CSV data with escaped delimiters and special characters, specifically "a![!|!]b![|]c[|]xyz\r\nabc[abc][|]xyz" which includes escaped bracket sequences and carriage return line feed separators. Parse this string using the configured CSV format by creating a parser with a string reader as the input source. Retrieve the first CSV record from the parser and assert that the first field equals "a[|]b![|]c" and the second field equals "xyz", verifying that the escape character properly handles the multi-character delimiter. Advance to the second record and assert that its first field equals "abc[abc]" and the second field equals "xyz", confirming that unescaped delimiters correctly separate fields while escaped sequences are preserved as literal text. The test uses JUnit framework for assertions.

Initialize a string variable containing CSV data with multi-character delimiter "[|]" and escape character '!' sequences, specifically "a![!|!]b![|]c[|]xyz\r\nabc[abc][|]xyz" which represents two records where the first record has escaped delimiters and the second has a literal delimiter. Create a CSVFormat instance by calling the builder method on CSVFormat.DEFAULT, then call setDelimiter with the string "[|]" to configure a multi-character delimiter, followed by setEscape with the character '!' to set the escape character, and finally call get to build the format. Parse the CSV data by calling the parse method on the CSVFormat instance, passing a new StringReader constructed with the source string, and wrap this in a try-with-resources statement to ensure proper resource cleanup. Retrieve the first CSV record by calling nextRecord on the CSVParser and assert that the first field (index 0) equals "a[|]b![|]c" using assertEquals, verifying that the escaped delimiter sequences were properly unescaped while the literal escape sequence remained intact. Assert that the second field (index 1) equals "xyz" using assertEquals to confirm proper field separation. Retrieve the second CSV record by calling nextRecord again and assert that its first field (index 0) equals "abc[abc]" using assertEquals, confirming that the literal delimiter was correctly parsed as field content. Assert that the second field (index 1) of the second record equals "xyz" using assertEquals to validate the final field parsing. The test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that character position tracking correctly accounts for comment lines when parsing CSV data with comments enabled. Initialize a CSV format configuration that designates a hash symbol as the comment marker, enables header parsing, and skips the header record during processing. Create CSV content containing multiple comment lines interspersed with header and data records, where comments appear before the header, between data records, and at the end. Parse this content using the configured format and iterate through the resulting records. For each record retrieved, assert that its character position corresponds to the starting position of the comment line that immediately precedes it in the original CSV content, verifying that the parser correctly tracks character positions even when comment lines are present and processed. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the character position tracking functionality of a CSV parser when processing files containing comment lines. Initialize a CSV string containing multiple comment lines (marked with hash symbols) interspersed with header and data records, specifically including comments before the header, between data rows, and at the end. Create a CSV format configuration using the default format builder, setting the comment marker to hash, enabling header parsing, and configuring the parser to skip the header record. Parse the CSV string using a string reader with the configured format, then iterate through the resulting records using the parser's iterator. For each record retrieved, call the character position method and assert that it equals the index position of the preceding comment line within the original CSV string, verifying that the parser correctly tracks character positions relative to comment boundaries rather than data boundaries. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that CSV data containing escape characters can be correctly written and then parsed back to preserve the original values. Initialize a CSV format configuration with the default settings but specify a backslash as the escape character. Create a string writer to capture the output, then construct a CSV printer using the writer and format configuration. Print a single record containing two values: a string with a trailing backslash followed by a space, and a simple string value. Close the printer to finalize the output. Create a string reader from the captured output and construct a CSV parser using the same format configuration. Parse all records from the string reader and close the parser. Iterate through the parsed records and verify that the first field matches the original string with the trailing backslash and space, and the second field matches the simple string value, confirming that the escape character handling preserves the data integrity during the round-trip process. The testing framework used is JUnit.

This test validates the parsing functionality when using a multi-character delimiter combined with escape sequences. Initialize a format configuration that uses a multi-character delimiter pattern and sets an escape character for handling special sequences within the data. Create a parser using this format to process input containing values that include both the delimiter pattern and escaped sequences, where some delimiters are escaped and should be treated as literal text rather than field separators. Parse the input to extract records and verify that the parser correctly distinguishes between actual delimiters and escaped delimiter sequences, ensuring that escaped delimiters are preserved as part of the field values while unescaped delimiters properly separate the fields. Assert that the parsed records contain the expected field values with escaped sequences properly converted to their literal representations and that field boundaries are correctly identified despite the complex delimiter and escape patterns. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a StringReader with CSV content containing three columns where the header row is "header1,null,header3" and two data rows are "1,2,3" and "4,5,6", then create a CSVParser using CSVFormat DEFAULT configuration with header parsing enabled, null string set to "null", and missing column names allowed. Parse the CSV content using the parse method on the configured format, then obtain an iterator from the parser and retrieve the first CSVRecord using the iterator's next method. From the first record, call getParser to obtain the CSVParser instance, then verify that getHeaderNames returns a list containing only "header1" and "header3" using assertEquals with Arrays.asList, and assert that getHeaderMap returns a map with size 2 using assertEquals. The test validates that when a header column contains the configured null string value, that column is excluded from both the header names list and header map, demonstrating proper handling of null column names in CSV parsing when allowMissingColumnNames is enabled. This test uses the JUnit testing framework with @Test annotation.

This test validates that two CSV format configurations with different header column orders are not considered equal. Initialize a CSV format configuration with a single quote delimiter, carriage return record separator, hash comment marker, plus escape character, headers in the order "One", "Two", "Three", and various formatting options including ignoring empty lines and surrounding spaces, double quote character, and quote-all mode. Create a second format configuration by copying the first and modifying only the header order to "Three", "Two", "One" while keeping all other settings identical. Verify that the equality comparison between these two configurations returns false, confirming that header column order affects format equality. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a CSV string containing comment lines interspersed with data records, specifically setting up a multi-line CSV with "# Comment1" followed by "Header1,Header2", then "# Comment2", "Value1,Value2", "# Comment3", "Value3,Value4", and finally "# Comment4". Create a CSVFormat instance by calling the builder method on the DEFAULT format, then configure it to use the hash character as the comment marker by calling setCommentMarker, enable header parsing by calling setHeader with no arguments, set skip header record to true by calling setSkipHeaderRecord, and finalize the format by calling get. Parse the CSV string using the configured format by calling the parse method with a new StringReader wrapping the CSV string, which returns a CSVParser instance. Within a try-with-resources block to ensure proper resource management, obtain an iterator from the parser by calling iterator, then retrieve the first record by calling next on the iterator and store it as the first CSVRecord. Assert that the character position of the first record equals the index position of "# Comment2" within the original CSV string by calling getCharacterPosition on the first record and comparing it to the result of calling indexOf with "# Comment2" on the CSV string using assertEquals. Retrieve the second record by calling next again on the iterator and store it as the second CSVRecord. Assert that the character position of the second record equals the index position of "# Comment3" within the original CSV string by calling getCharacterPosition on the second record and comparing it to the result of calling indexOf with "# Comment3" on the CSV string using assertEquals. This test validates that the CSVRecord getCharacterPosition method correctly returns the character position where each record begins in the source CSV data, specifically testing that comment lines preceding data records are properly accounted for in the position calculation when comments are enabled in the CSV format configuration. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation.

Initialize a CSV format with default settings, then configure it to use headers, set the null string to "null", and allow missing column names. Create a string reader containing CSV data with headers "header1,null,header3" followed by two data rows "1,2,3" and "4,5,6", where the second column header is the literal string "null" which should be interpreted as a null value. Parse the CSV data using the configured format, then iterate through the records to get the first record. Retrieve the parser from the record and assert that the header names list contains only "header1" and "header3", verifying that the null column name was properly excluded. Additionally, assert that the header map size is 2, confirming that only the non-null headers are included in the mapping. This test validates that the CSV parser correctly handles null column names in headers when the allow missing column names option is enabled, ensuring that null headers are filtered out from both the header names list and header map. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a CSV format configuration by creating a new format with a single quote delimiter and building it with specific settings including a carriage return record separator, hash comment marker, plus escape character, header columns named "One", "Two", and "Three", enabled empty line ignoring, enabled surrounding space ignoring, double quote character, and quote mode set to ALL. Create a second CSV format by taking the builder from the first format and modifying only the header to reverse the column order to "Three", "Two", "One". Assert that the two CSV format objects are not equal to each other using a helper method that performs bidirectional inequality checks. This test validates that CSV format equality is sensitive to header column ordering and uses the JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a test to verify CSV parsing and printing functionality with escape character handling for a specific JIRA issue CSV-249. Create a CSVFormat instance using the DEFAULT format builder, configure it with a backslash escape character by calling setEscape with the backslash character, and retrieve the format using get. Instantiate a StringWriter to capture output, then create a CSVPrinter using the StringWriter and the configured format within a try-with-resources block. Use the CSVPrinter's printRecord method to output a record containing two values: the string "foo \\" (foo followed by a space and backslash) and the string "bar". After the printer is closed, create a StringReader initialized with the StringWriter's string content. Establish a CSVParser using the parser builder, configure it with the StringReader as the reader and the same CSVFormat, then retrieve the parser using get within another try-with-resources block. Call the parser's getRecords method to obtain a List of CSVRecord objects. Iterate through the records using forEach with a lambda expression that performs two assertEquals assertions: first verify that the first field (index 0) of each record equals "foo \\" using the CSVRecord's get method, and second verify that the second field (index 1) equals "bar". The test validates that CSV data with escape characters is correctly written and subsequently parsed, ensuring the escape character properly handles the backslash in the output and maintains data integrity during the round-trip process. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that the expression parser correctly detects and rejects variable redefinition within the same scope. Initialize a source string containing a try-with-resources statement that declares a variable in the resource section and then attempts to redeclare the same variable within the try block body. Create a script from this source string using the expression engine, expecting this operation to throw a parsing exception due to the variable redefinition conflict. Assert that the thrown exception is specifically a parsing exception and verify that its error message contains text indicating that the variable is already declared. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

     *  java.util.*

    • *

    • *

description: This test validates the stack overflow detection and handling capabilities of the expression evaluation engine when processing recursive function calls. Initialize a script engine with strict mode, safe mode, and a stack overflow limit of 5 levels, then create an execution context and define a recursive factorial function script that takes a parameter. Execute the script with a small input value and verify the factorial calculation returns the expected result. Next, execute the same script with a larger input that exceeds the stack limit and confirm that a stack overflow exception is thrown, verifying the exception message contains "jexl" to indicate engine-level detection. Then reconfigure the engine to strict mode only without the stack overflow limit, create a new recursive script without proper termination conditions, execute it with a large input, and verify that a different stack overflow exception is thrown with a message containing "jvm" to indicate system-level detection. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the execution of a JEXL stream processing expression that performs mathematical operations on a list of mixed-type elements. Initialize a string variable with the value "$0.map(x -> x * x).reduce((a, x) -> a + x)" which represents a JEXL expression that maps each element to its square and then reduces the results by summing them. Create a JexlEngine instance using JexlBuilder with safe mode disabled by calling the safe method with false and then create. Instantiate a JexlInfo object with the parameters "testStream", 1, and 1 to provide debugging information. Create a MapContext instance using the StreamContext constructor which serves as the execution context for variable resolution. Generate a JexlScript by calling createScript on the engine with the source string and the parameter name "$0". Execute the script by calling the execute method on the script object, passing the context and a list created from Arrays.asList containing the values 1, 2d, and "3" as arguments. Assert that the returned result equals 14.0d with a delta tolerance of 0.00001d using assertEquals, which validates that the stream operations correctly squared each element (1*1=1, 2*2=4, 3*3=9) and summed them (1+4+9=14). This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

Initialize a JEXL engine with strict mode enabled, safe mode enabled, and a stack overflow limit of 5, then create a map context for variable storage. Create a script that defines a recursive factorial function using lambda syntax with parameter "a", where the function calculates factorial by multiplying the input by the result of calling itself with the decremented value, with a base case when the input is 1 or less. Execute the script with the context and argument value 3, then assert that the result equals 6. Next, execute the same script with argument value 32 and assert that a JexlException.StackOverflow exception is thrown, then verify that the exception's string representation contains "jexl". Create a second JEXL engine with only strict mode enabled (no stack overflow limit), then create another script with a recursive function that lacks a proper base case and will recurse indefinitely. Execute this second script with argument value 32, assert that a JexlException.StackOverflow exception is thrown, and verify that this exception's string representation contains "jvm". This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that expression evaluation correctly handles property access failures and throws appropriate exceptions when accessing non-existent or unsolvable properties in strict mode. Initialize a context and populate it with a test object that has a configurable property, then create an expression engine configured for strict evaluation with safety and silence disabled. Create three expressions that represent different levels of property access depth on the test object. For each test scenario involving both null and non-null property values, set the object's property to the test value and verify that direct property access succeeds by comparing the retrieved value with the expected result. Then assert that accessing a non-existent property on the object throws a property exception, and similarly verify that attempting to access a nested property through the non-existent property also throws a property exception, confirming that the engine properly detects and reports unsolvable property chains in strict mode. This test uses JUnit 5 testing framework.

This test validates the serialization and deserialization functionality of CSVRecord objects by creating a CSV parser with specific format configurations and verifying that serialized records maintain their essential data while losing parser-dependent functionality. Initialize a CSVParser by calling the parse method on CSVParser class with the input string "A,B\n#my comment\nOne,Two" and a CSVFormat configured with DEFAULT settings, withHeader method called with no arguments, and withCommentMarker method called with the '#' character, then retrieve the first record using the iterator's next method and store it in a variable. Create a ByteArrayOutputStream and wrap it with an ObjectOutputStream, then serialize the CSVRecord by calling writeObject method on the ObjectOutputStream with the record as the argument, and close the ObjectOutputStream. Create a ByteArrayInputStream from the serialized byte array using toByteArray method on the ByteArrayOutputStream, wrap it with an ObjectInputStream, and deserialize the object by calling readObject method, then close the ObjectInputStream. Assert that the deserialized object is an instance of CSVRecord class using assertInstanceOf method, then cast it to CSVRecord type and verify the record's core data integrity by asserting that getRecordNumber returns 1L, get method with index 0 returns "One", get method with index 1 returns "Two", size method returns 2, getCharacterPosition matches the original record's character position, and getComment returns "my comment". Verify that parser-dependent functionality is properly disabled by asserting that getParser returns null using a comment indicating the parser is not serialized, isConsistent returns true, isMapped method with "A" returns false, isSet method with "A" returns false, and toMap method returns a map with size 0. Finally, confirm that accessing header-based functionality throws an IllegalStateException by using assertThrows method to verify that calling get method with "A" as the string argument raises this exception. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the currying functionality of expression scripts that accept multiple parameters and can be progressively bound with arguments. Initialize an expression engine and create a lambda script that takes three parameters and returns their sum. Apply currying to the base script by binding the first two parameters with specific numeric values, then verify that the resulting script has only one remaining unbound parameter. Continue the currying process by binding the final parameter with another numeric value, then execute the fully curried script without any context to confirm it produces the expected sum of all three originally bound values. Assert that the parameter count decreases correctly after each currying step and that the final execution yields the arithmetic total of the bound arguments. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a map context and a test object with a bar property, then set the test object in the context under a variable name. Configure a JEXL engine with strict mode enabled, safe mode disabled, and silent mode disabled to ensure exceptions are thrown for property access errors. Create three JEXL expressions for property access patterns: one for direct property access, one for accessing a non-existent property on the test object, and one for chained property access through the non-existent property. Set up an array containing null and an integer value as test arguments. For each argument value, set the test object's bar property to the current argument value, then evaluate the direct property access expression and assert it returns the expected bar value. Next, evaluate the expression accessing the non-existent property and assert it throws a JexlException.Property since the property cannot be resolved. description: This test validates the behavior of JEXL expression evaluation for negated string prefix and suffix operations using an asserter component. Initialize an asserter instance with JEXL engine support and configure it to operate in non-strict mode. Set a variable with a dotted name to the string value "foobar" and assert that the expression checking if the string does not start with "foo" evaluates to false, then assert that the expression checking if the string does not end with "foo" evaluates to true. Update the same variable to contain "barfoo" and verify that the expression for not starting with "foo" now evaluates to true, while the expression for not ending with "foo" evaluates to false. The assertions validate that the negated prefix operator correctly identifies when strings do not begin with specified substrings and the negated suffix operator properly determines when strings do not end with given substrings. This test uses JUnit as the testing framework.

description: Initialize a CSV parser with a default format that includes headers for columns A, B, and C, and configure it to skip the header record while parsing a string containing comma-separated values with two data rows where the first row has only two values and the second row has three values. Create the parser using a string reader containing the data "a,b,c\n1,2\nx,y,z" and set up the format to use the specified headers and skip the first line. Iterate through the parser to retrieve the first CSV record and verify that all three columns A, B, and C are mapped using the isMapped method, then check that columns A and B are set while column C is not set using the isSet method. Assert that the values for columns A and B are "1" and "2" respectively using the get method, and confirm the record is not consistent using the isConsistent method. Retrieve the second CSV record and verify that all three columns are both mapped and set, assert that the values are "x", "y", and "z" for columns A, B, and C respectively, and confirm this record is consistent. Finally, assert that no additional records remain in the iterator. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the dynamic creation and execution of classes with customizable constructor behavior through a scripting engine. Initialize a temporary directory for file operations and set up a context with a numeric value. Create a class generator with a specific seed and define constructor body logic that retrieves the context value and adds an offset to initialize the class field. Generate and compile the first class, then verify the class loader relationship and class name match expectations. Instantiate the class using the context and confirm the result type. Configure the scripting engine to use the generated class loader and clear the generator state. Execute a script that creates new instances of the class by name or class reference and validate that the constructor logic produces the expected calculated value. Recreate the same class with different constructor logic using the same seed, ensuring the new class has the same name but is a different class instance. Instantiate the updated class and verify its type. Update the scripting engine's class loader to use the new class and execute the same script again, confirming that the updated constructor logic now produces the different expected calculated value when invoked with both class name and class reference. Clean up the temporary directory after completion. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the dynamic class creation and script execution capabilities of the JEXL expression engine with runtime class loading. Initialize a JEXL context with an integer value of 1000, then create a class creator utility with a seed value of 1 and configure its constructor body to retrieve the context value and add 10 to initialize an instance field. Generate and compile the dynamic class, assert that the class loader and simple name match expectations, and create an instance using the context to verify the class type. Set the JEXL engine's class loader to the dynamic class loader and clear the creator state. Create a JEXL script that constructs new instances using either class objects or class names and retrieves their value field, then execute the script with both the class object and class name as arguments, asserting that both return 1010. Recreate the same class with a modified constructor body that adds 99 instead of 10, verify the new class has the same name but is a different object, create an instance of the updated class, and update the JEXL engine's class loader. Execute the same script again with both the class name and class object, asserting that both now return 1099 to demonstrate dynamic class reloading. The test uses JUnit framework for assertions and test execution.

This test validates that expression evaluation handles null method calls gracefully when both strict and silent modes are enabled. Initialize an expression engine with default settings, then create a map-based variable context and wrap it in an evaluation context that provides access to engine options. Configure the evaluation options to enable both strict mode for unknown variables and silent mode to suppress exceptions. Create a script that attempts to call a method on an undefined variable, then execute it and assert that the result is null since the variable doesn't exist. Next, define the variable with a string value, execute the same script again, and verify that it returns the expected hash code of the string. Create another script that references the method without parentheses and confirm it also returns null when executed. Clear the variable context and repeat the same sequence using expressions instead of scripts - create an expression for the method call, evaluate it with the undefined variable and assert null is returned, then set the variable and verify the hash code is returned correctly, and finally test the method reference without parentheses returns null. This testing uses the JUnit framework.

Initialize a CSV format configuration by creating a new format with a single quote delimiter and building it with specific settings including a carriage return record separator, hash comment marker, plus escape character, and enabling options to ignore empty lines and surrounding spaces, then set the quote character to double quote, quote mode to ALL, and null string to "null". Create a second CSV format by taking the builder from the first format and modifying only the null string to "---". Assert that the two formats are not equal using a helper method that performs bidirectional inequality checks. This test validates that CSV format objects with different null string configurations are properly distinguished as unequal instances. The testing is performed using JUnit assertions.

This test validates the behavior of a JEXL expression engine when executing scripts and expressions that reference undefined variables in strict and silent mode. Initialize a JEXL engine with strict and silent options enabled, create a map context for variable storage, and wrap it in an evaluation context with engine options configured for strict and silent evaluation. Create a script that calls the hashCode method on an undefined variable named "dummy" and execute it, asserting that the result is null since the variable is undefined and silent mode prevents exceptions. Set the "dummy" variable to the string "abcd" in the context and execute the same script again, asserting that the result equals the hash code of "abcd". Create another script that references the hashCode property (without method invocation) on the undefined variable and execute it, asserting the result is null. Clear the context variables and repeat the same sequence of operations using JEXL expressions instead of scripts - create an expression for "dummy.hashCode()", evaluate it with an empty context and assert null, then set "dummy" to "abcd" and assert the evaluation equals the hash code of "abcd", and finally create an expression for the "dummy.hashCode" property and assert it evaluates to null. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that a sandboxed template engine properly restricts access to specific classes while still allowing template evaluation with lambda expressions and variable substitution. Initialize a specialized introspection component that blocks access to certain framework classes, then configure an engine with this restricted introspection capability and create a template engine from it. Set up a custom evaluation context that supports lambda execution functionality. Create a template from a multi-line string that defines a variable, executes a lambda expression with parameters, and outputs formatted content containing the variable and lambda parameters. Evaluate the template using the custom context with a numeric argument, capturing the output through a string writer. Assert that the final output matches the expected formatted string containing the variable value and the provided argument. The test uses JUnit 5 with parameterized testing.

Initialize a CSV format configuration by creating a new format with a single quote delimiter and configuring it with carriage return record separator, hash comment marker, plus escape character, ignore empty lines enabled, ignore surrounding spaces enabled, double quote character, quote mode set to ALL, null string as "null", and skip header record enabled. Create a second format by copying the first format and modifying it to disable the skip header record setting by passing false to the skip header record method. Assert that the two format objects are not equal using a helper assertion method that validates inequality in both directions. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the dynamic class creation and instantiation functionality within the JEXL expression evaluation framework, specifically testing the ability to create classes with custom constructors that can be invoked through JEXL scripts and subsequently recreated with different behaviors. Initialize a MapContext instance and set a variable named value to the integer 1000, then create a ClassCreator instance using the jexl field of the test class and the base File field. Configure the ClassCreator by calling setSeed with the value 1 to establish the class name as foo1 and set up the package directory structure, then call setCtorBody with a constructor body string that assigns the context value plus 10 to an instance field. Invoke createClass with true to generate, compile, and load the dynamic class, then assert that the class loader of the resulting Class object matches the ClassLoader returned by getClassLoader on the ClassCreator, and verify the simple class name equals foo1. Create an instance of the dynamic class by calling newInstance on the ClassCreator with the class and context, then assert the instance's class matches the original class. Set the JEXL engine's class loader to the ClassCreator's class loader using setClassLoader, then call clear on the ClassCreator to reset its state. Create a JexlScript by calling createScript on the jexl engine with a lambda expression that constructs a new instance using the provided class parameter and accesses its value field. Execute the script twice with the context and different parameters: first with the Class object itself, asserting the result equals 1010, then with the class name string, again asserting the result equals 1010. Reconfigure the ClassCreator by calling setSeed with 1 again and setCtorBody with a different constructor body that adds 99 instead of 10 to the context value, then create a new class using createClass with true. Verify the new class has the same simple name foo1 but is not the same object as the original class using assertNotSame, then create an instance of the new class and assert its class type. Update the JEXL engine's class loader to the new class's loader and execute the script again with both the class name and Class object, asserting both results equal 1099 to demonstrate the dynamic class replacement functionality. The test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the Test annotation.

This test validates the behavior of JEXL expression and script evaluation when handling null method calls in strict and silent mode configurations. Initialize a JexlEngine instance using the createEngine method with a false parameter, then create a MapContext instance for variable storage and wrap it in a JexlEvalContext to manage evaluation options. Create a JexlScript using createScript with the expression "dummy.hashCode()" and execute it with the context using the execute method, then assert that the result is null using assertNull with the script's getSourceText method as the error message supplier. Set a variable named "dummy" to the string "abcd" in the context using the set method, execute the same script again, and assert that the result equals the integer value of "abcd".hashCode() using assertEquals. Create another script with "dummy.hashCode" (without parentheses), execute it, and assert the result is null. Clear all variables from the MapContext using the clear method, then create a JexlExpression using createExpression with "dummy.hashCode()" and evaluate it with the context using the evaluate method, asserting the result is null with the expression's toString method as the error message. Set "dummy" to "abcd" again, evaluate the expression, and assert the result equals the integer hashCode value. Finally, create an expression with "dummy.hashCode" (without parentheses), evaluate it, and assert the result is null. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation.

Construct a new JEXL engine with the custom uberspect and create a template engine from it. Initialize a specialized context instance (Context311) for the evaluation. Define a template string containing JEXL script directives and expressions that declares a variable, executes a lambda function with parameters, and outputs formatted content including the variable and lambda parameters. Create a template from the string using the template engine with a string reader and double-dollar prefix. Initialize a string writer for capturing output and evaluate the template with the context, writer, and an integer argument of 42. Retrieve the generated output string from the writer and assert that it equals the expected formatted result containing "Universe" and "42" with proper HTML paragraph tags and newline formatting. The test uses JUnit 5 with parameterized testing via MethodSource annotation.

This test validates variable scoping behavior in a script execution environment with conditional declarations and lexical scope controls. Next, disable lexical scoping in the options and create a script that defines a function with conditional variable declarations in different branches, executing it with various parameters to verify the conditional variables are accessible outside their declaration blocks. Re-enable strict mode and confirm that accessing an undefined variable throws an exception containing the variable name in the error message. Finally, disable strict mode and verify that accessing the undefined variable returns null instead of throwing an exception. The testing framework used is JUnit.

Initialize a JEXL evaluation context and retrieve its engine options, then create a JEXL engine with strict mode enabled. description: This test validates the permission system's ability to correctly allow or deny access to various Java reflection elements based on a parsed permission configuration. The test exercises the JexlPermissions class's allow method with different types of reflection objects and verifies that the permission rules are properly enforced through boolean assertions. Initialize the test by calling the permissions0 helper method which creates a JexlPermissions object by parsing a string configuration that defines access rules for specific packages, classes, methods, fields, and constructors within the org.apache.commons.jexl3.internal.introspection namespace, then pass this permissions object to the runTestPermissions helper method. Within the helper method, first assert that the allow method returns false when passed null values for Field, Package, Method, Constructor, and Class types to verify null safety. Next, test class-level permissions by asserting that the allow method returns false for the A2 class but returns true for both A3 and A5 classes. Proceed to test method permissions by retrieving Method objects using getMethod and getDeclaredMethod from classes A, A0, A1, and A2, asserting that each retrieval is not null, then verifying that only the method from class A is allowed while methods from A0, A1, and A2 are denied. Continue with field permission testing by obtaining Field objects for field i from class A, field i0 from class A0, and field i1 from class A1, asserting non-null retrieval for each, then confirming that only the field from class A is permitted while fields from A0 and A1 are rejected. Finally, test constructor permissions by retrieving Constructor objects from classes A, A0, and A3 using getConstructor and getDeclaredConstructor, asserting non-null for each retrieval, then validating that only the constructor from class A is allowed while constructors from A0 and A3 are denied. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

Initialize a JexlEngine instance by calling the createEngine method with a false parameter to configure the engine without specific features, then create a JexlScript by calling createScript on the engine with a lambda expression string that defines a function taking parameter x and returning x multiplied by 6. Create a JexlEvalContext instance to serve as the evaluation context, then retrieve the JexlOptions from this context by calling getEngineOptions. Configure the options to ensure errors will be thrown by calling setSilent with false, make unknown variables throw exceptions by calling setStrict with true, and enable strict arithmetic mode by calling setStrictArithmetic with true to prevent null operand operations. Execute the script with the empty context and no arguments by calling execute on the script with the context, expecting this to throw a JexlException due to the undefined variable x in strict mode, and use assertThrows to verify that a JexlException is thrown during execution. Retrieve the exception message by calling getMessage on the caught exception and assert that the message contains the string "null" by using assertTrue with indexOf to verify the null reference is mentioned in the error message. Modify the arithmetic strictness by calling setStrictArithmetic with false to allow null operands, then execute the script again with the context and a null argument by calling execute with the context and a null Object parameter, and assert that the result equals 0 using assertEquals to verify that null multiplication returns zero when strict arithmetic is disabled. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the Test annotation.

This test validates the evaluation of JEXL template expressions containing map literals and size function calls. Initialize a JEXL builder and use it to configure the engine and template engine through a helper method that sets up the necessary components. Create a null context reference and define a template expression source string that contains a map literal with two key-value pairs (map with value 123 and map2 with value 456) wrapped in a size function call. Use the template engine to create an expression from this source string, then evaluate the expression with the null context to obtain the result. Assert that the expression is marked as immediate using the isImmediate method, verify that the evaluation result equals the integer 2 (representing the size of the map), and confirm that the original source string matches the extracted source from the expression's string representation using a helper method that parses the source from formatted output. The test uses JUnit 5 with parameterized testing via MethodSource annotation.

description: This test validates the behavior of expression evaluation when using specialized arithmetic for handling document nodes. Initialize an evaluation context and create an expression engine configured with strict mode enabled, safe mode disabled, and custom arithmetic designed for processing document structures. Create multiple script expressions that test emptiness checking and size calculation operations on document nodes, using both method-style and function-style syntax. Execute the emptiness and size scripts with null inputs to verify they return true for emptiness and zero for size when no document is provided. Test the scripts with safe mode enabled in the context options to ensure null handling returns appropriate null values instead of throwing exceptions. Create document structures with varying content including nodes with attributes only, nodes with child elements, and empty nodes, then execute the emptiness and size scripts against each document type to verify correct detection of empty versus non-empty states and accurate child element counting. Additionally, test attribute modification capabilities by creating a document with an attribute, setting up a context with the document node and a new value, then executing a script that attempts to modify the attribute value and verify the change is reflected in the document structure, noting that this operation may fail on newer Java versions due to module restrictions. The testing uses JUnit framework for assertions and exception handling.

Initialize a JEXL builder and create a JEXL engine with a reference uberspect wrapping the default uberspect, an optional arithmetic instance, and safe mode disabled. Create a JEXL info object with test name and line/column coordinates, then initialize a stream context as the execution context. Create a script from a source string containing a stream operation that maps elements to their squares and reduces them by addition, with a parameter placeholder for the input collection. Execute the script with the context and an integer list containing values 1, 2, and 3 as the argument. Assert that the execution result equals the integer 14, which represents the sum of squares (1 + 4 + 9). This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

Construct a map context for variable storage and create debugging information for script execution. Parse a script containing a stream operation that maps each element to its square and reduces the results by summing them, using a parameter placeholder for the input data. Execute the script with a list of integers as the argument and verify that the result equals the expected sum of squares. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the functionality of class hierarchy analysis and array type determination within an expression evaluation framework. Initialize an array builder with a fixed capacity and configure an expression engine with script features disabled to create an expression-only evaluation environment. Retrieve the complete inheritance hierarchy for a specific test class and verify that the returned collection contains the expected number of superclasses and interfaces, then validate that these types are returned in the correct hierarchical order by comparing against a predefined sequence of parent classes and interfaces. Test the common superclass computation functionality by finding the shared ancestor between different class pairs, ensuring that the algorithm correctly identifies the most specific common parent class for various inheritance scenarios including both custom test classes and standard collection types. Verify that the superclass analysis works correctly with built-in Java collection classes by computing their common ancestors and confirming the results include expected abstract collection types and interfaces. Create test objects from different classes in the inheritance hierarchy and use the expression engine to evaluate array creation scripts with these objects as parameters, then validate that the resulting arrays have component types that match the computed common superclass for the provided object combinations, testing scenarios where objects share specific common ancestors versus more general base types. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the XML arithmetic functionality of a JEXL expression engine by initializing a JEXL engine with strict mode enabled, safe mode disabled, and a custom XML arithmetic handler, then creating multiple scripts to test empty and size operations on XML nodes through both method call and function call syntax. Initialize variables for XML documents, nodes, boolean results, and integer sizes, then create four scripts that test node emptiness and size using expressions like "x.empty()", "empty(x)", "x.size()", and "size(x)" with a single parameter. description: Initialize a StringReader with CSV data containing three lines: a header line "a,b,c", a data line "1,2" with only two values, and a complete data line "x,y,z" with three values. Create a CSVParser using CSVFormat DEFAULT format configured with headers "A", "B", "C" and withSkipHeaderRecord enabled to skip the first line, then parse the StringReader input. Obtain an iterator from the parser and retrieve the first CSVRecord by calling next on the iterator. Assert that the record isMapped returns true for columns "A", "B", and "C", confirming all three headers are mapped. Assert that isSet returns true for columns "A" and "B" since they have values, but false for column "C" since no third value exists in the first data record. Verify the actual values by asserting that get method returns "1" for column "A" and "2" for column "B". Assert that isConsistent returns false for this first record because it has only two values while three headers are defined. Retrieve the second CSVRecord by calling next again on the iterator. Assert that isMapped returns true for all three columns "A", "B", and "C" for this second record as well. Assert that isSet returns true for all three columns "A", "B", and "C" since this record contains three values. Verify the values by asserting that get returns "x" for column "A", "y" for column "B", and "z" for column "C". Assert that isConsistent returns true for this second record since it has three values matching the three defined headers. Finally, assert that the iterator hasNext returns false, confirming no more records exist. The test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the class hierarchy analysis and array type inference capabilities of the class miscellaneous utilities and expression engine components. Initialize an array builder with capacity 1, then create a JEXL engine with script features disabled to handle expressions with arguments. Retrieve the superclass hierarchy for ClassC using the class miscellaneous utility and assert that the returned set contains multiple classes, then verify the ordering matches the expected sequence of ClassB, ClassA, Class0, InterC, InterX, InterB, InterA, and Inter0 by iterating through the superclass set and comparing each element. Test common superclass determination by finding the intersection between ClassC and ClassX which should return Class0, then between ClassC and ClassB which should return ClassB, and between ArrayList and ArrayDeque which should return AbstractCollection. Obtain the superclass set for ArrayList and ArrayDeque, assert it is not empty, and verify it contains the expected classes AbstractCollection, Collection, Iterable, Cloneable, and Serializable. Determine the common superclass between ArrayList and the class of an empty list, expecting AbstractList as the result, then find the first superclass from their hierarchy. Create instances of ClassA with value 1, ClassB with value 2, ClassC with value 3, and ClassX with value 4, then create a JEXL script that builds an array from four parameters. Execute the script with various combinations of these objects to test array type inference: passing a, b, c, c should produce an array with ClassA component type, while passing a, b, c, x should yield Class0 component type, and x, c, b, a should also result in Class0 component type. Create a ClassD instance and execute the script with a, b, c, d to verify the array has Inter0 component type. Finally, create a script with extended array syntax and execute it with a, b, c, c to assert the result is a List instance. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.
